Empirical Research Plan: The Causal Return to Schooling Using Identical Twins  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: 2-stage least squares (IV) within–monozygotic-twin fixed effects (or first-difference) design.  
Why appropriate:  
• Twin fixed effects remove all time-invariant family background, genetic ability, and shared early-life environment.  
• An IV is required because self-reported schooling is measured with classical noise that biases the within-twin coefficient toward zero.  
• One twin’s report of the other twin’s schooling is highly correlated with the true, but plausibly uncorrelated with the idiosyncratic wage error, satisfying relevance and (conditional on FE) exclusion.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: Years of schooling (continuous). In the differenced specification, ΔEdu ≡ Edu_selfA – Edu_selfB. “Treated” twins are those with ΔEdu > 0.  
Control group: Their genetically-identical co-twin with lower schooling (ΔEdu < 0).  
Timing: Schooling is completed prior to the wage observation (survey).  
No discrete cutoff → not an RDD.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1  (Twin FE validity) – After differencing, all remaining unobservables that affect both ΔEdu and Δwage are zero-mean and uncorrelated with ΔEdu.  
Plausibility: strong for genetics and family background, weaker for non-shared post-birth shocks (e.g., illness) that influence both education and earnings.  

A2  (Instrument relevance) – Twin B’s report of Twin A’s schooling (Edu_repBA) is correlated with Twin A’s true schooling.  
Plausibility: siblings generally know each other’s schooling; first-stage F-stat can be directly tested.  

A3  (Instrument exogeneity / exclusion) – Conditional on true schooling and twin FE, Edu_repBA affects Twin A’s wage only through actual education.  
Plausibility: Reporting errors should not systematically affect wages; cannot raise wages mechanically.  

A4  (Measurement-error independence) – Reporting errors are not perfectly correlated across twins.  
Plausibility: Interviewed separately; random recall errors.  

A5  (SUTVA) – Twin B’s education affects Twin A’s wage only via Twin A’s own schooling.  
Plausibility: Some labour-market spillovers could exist but likely tiny within a national labour market.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

Threat 1: Non-shared ability/health shocks simultaneously lower schooling and wages (violates A1).  
Mitigation:  
• Control for current health status and occupation type.  
• Sensitivity analysis dropping pairs where schooling gaps arose from documented illness/parental leave (survey questions).  

Threat 2: Correlated mis-reporting (violates A4) — twins may copy responses or attend interview together.  
Mitigation:  
• Use interviewer notes to drop pairs interviewed jointly.  
• Compute correlation of self-report and co-report errors; if high, show attenuation-robust bounds (e.g., Hausman, 2001).  

Threat 3: Sample selection – attending the Twinsburg Festival is non-random.  
Mitigation:  
• Compare observable characteristics (age, schooling levels) with representative twin registries (e.g., National Longitudinal Survey of Youth MZ subsample) to show external validity.  
• Discuss that causal internal validity is unaffected if selection is unrelated to within-pair education gaps.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE/IV
library(AER)          # ivreg robustness
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("princeton_twins_survey.csv")   # assume each row = individual twin

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------
# Create twin-pair identifier (already provided or build from family id)
# Assume variable pair_id exists
setorder(dt, pair_id)                  # sort
dt[,  educ_self := as.numeric(educ_self)]
dt[,  educ_corep := as.numeric(educ_reported_by_cotwin)]
dt[,  wage      := as.numeric(hourly_wage)]

# Keep complete cases on core vars
dt <- dt[!is.na(educ_self) & !is.na(educ_corep) & !is.na(wage)]

# 2a. First-difference within each pair
diff_dt <- dt[, .(
    d_wage  = wage[1]  - wage[2],
    d_educ  = educ_self[1]        - educ_self[2],
    d_iv    = educ_corep[1]       - educ_corep[2],
    age_mean= mean(age),
    male    = mean(sex=="male")
), by = pair_id]

# 3. Main specification: IV first-difference ----------------------------
iv_main <- feols(d_wage ~ 1 | 0 | (d_educ ~ d_iv), data = diff_dt,
                 vcov = "hetero")
summary(iv_main, cluster = ~pair_id)

# 4. OLS within-pair for comparison -------------------------------------
ols_fe <- feols(wage ~ educ_self | pair_id, data = dt, vcov = ~pair_id)
summary(ols_fe)

# 5. Robustness check: drop top/bottom 5% of ΔEdu -----------------------
p95 <- quantile(abs(diff_dt$d_educ), .95)
rb_dt <- diff_dt[abs(d_educ) <= p95]
iv_rb  <- feols(d_wage ~ 1 | 0 | (d_educ ~ d_iv), data = rb_dt,
                vcov = "hetero")
etable(list(Main = iv_main, Trim = iv_rb), se = "cluster")

# Additional robustness: use ivreg for weak-IV F-stat
ivreg_main <- ivreg(d_wage ~ d_educ | d_iv, data = diff_dt)
summary(ivreg_main, diagnostics = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
Prior: Each extra year of schooling raises hourly wages by ≈ 8–12 percent (log points). OLS without controls ≈ 10%; within-twin OLS attenuates to ≈ 4–6%; IV-corrected should rebound toward ≈ 8–10 percent. Direction unambiguously positive.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) ............................. 1  
C2: Instrument excludability (no direct wage effect) ...................... 0.8  
C3: Independence from pair-specific shocks ................................ 0.8  
C4: Measurement-error independence across twins ........................... 0.7  
C5: SUTVA (no wage spillovers within pair) ................................ 0.9  

Total ≈ 4.2 / 5 → strong but not perfect identification.
